title: Kian v. Florida
backgroundAndFacts:
Hamed Kian was convicted in Florida of a serious criminal offense after a jury trial. The case raises a fundamental question about what it means for a jury to be 'unanimous' under the U.S. Constitution. Specifically, the question is whether the Sixth Amendment requires that each individual juror be personally convinced beyond a reasonable doubt of every element of the charged crime, or whether it is enough that twelve jurors collectively agree on a guilty verdict even if individual jurors may have reached that verdict through different reasoning about different elements of the case.

This issue arises in the context of criminal offenses that have multiple ways they can be proven — for example, a crime that can be committed in two or three different ways. If six jurors believe the defendant committed the act one way, and six other jurors believe he committed it a different way, is that a truly unanimous verdict? Florida courts upheld Kian's conviction, finding that the jury's general verdict of guilty was constitutionally sufficient. Kian appealed, arguing that true unanimity requires each juror to agree on the same facts and same theory of guilt.

The Florida District Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, and the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear the case. The case has attracted enormous interest from across the legal spectrum, with amicus briefs filed by the United States, dozens of states, criminal defense organizations, civil rights groups, law professors, innocence projects, and victims' rights advocates.
legalQuestion: Whether the Sixth Amendment's guarantee of a unanimous jury verdict requires that every juror individually find each element of a crime proven beyond a reasonable doubt, or whether it is sufficient that the jury as a whole reach a unanimous verdict of guilty.
significance:
This case has major implications for criminal trials across the entire country. The Sixth Amendment's jury trial right — and particularly the unanimity requirement the Supreme Court extended to all states in Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) — could be significantly strengthened or clarified depending on how the Court rules. A ruling in Kian's favor could require courts to use specific jury instructions ensuring that every juror agrees on the same underlying facts and theory, not just the general verdict of guilty, potentially leading to more mistrials and retrials in cases involving crimes with multiple methods of commission.

Conversely, a ruling for Florida could preserve the longstanding practice of general verdicts and the flexibility that prosecutors rely on when charging crimes that can be committed in more than one way. The case touches on core principles of due process, the right to a fair trial, and the role of juries in the American justice system. The breadth of amicus participation — including the federal government, more than a dozen states on each side, leading constitutional law scholars, and major civil rights organizations — signals that the outcome will reshape how criminal trials are conducted nationwide.

parties.coreArgument: The Sixth Amendment's unanimity requirement demands that each juror individually find every element of the charged offense proven beyond a reasonable doubt, not merely that twelve jurors agree on a general verdict of guilty while potentially relying on different facts or theories. A verdict where jurors are divided on the key facts underlying guilt is not truly unanimous and violates the constitutional guarantee of a jury trial.
supportingPoints: The historical meaning of 'unanimous verdict' at the time of the Founding required juror agreement on the specific facts, not just the outcome.
Allowing jurors to agree on guilt through different and potentially inconsistent factual theories undermines the reasonable doubt standard for each element of the offense.
The Supreme Court's decision in Ramos v. Louisiana reaffirmed the deep constitutional roots of jury unanimity, which logically extends to agreement on the factual basis for the verdict.
Non-unanimous element-finding creates a serious risk of wrongful convictions, as no single theory of guilt may actually command the agreement of all twelve jurors.

parties.coreArgument: The Sixth Amendment's unanimity requirement is satisfied when all twelve jurors agree on a verdict of guilty, and does not mandate that every juror agree on the specific manner or means by which a crime was committed. General verdicts of guilty have been the accepted practice throughout American legal history, and imposing an element-specific unanimity requirement would be an unwarranted and disruptive expansion of the constitutional guarantee.
supportingPoints: The historical practice at common law and at the time of ratification permitted general guilty verdicts without requiring juror unanimity on each underlying theory of guilt.

Requiring element-by-element unanimity among individual jurors would impose an unprecedented burden on criminal prosecutions and could make it nearly impossible to convict defendants in cases involving alternative theories of guilt.
The Supreme Court has consistently distinguished between unanimity on the ultimate verdict and agreement on every factual detail, and has never imposed a constitutional requirement of the latter.
Numerous states and the federal government support Florida's interpretation, reflecting a settled national consensus that general verdicts satisfy the Sixth Amendment.

citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This is the most directly relevant precedent, as it held that the Sixth Amendment requires a unanimous jury verdict for conviction of a serious offense and applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment; both sides dispute how broadly its reasoning extends.

Held that jurors must unanimously agree on which specific violations make up a 'continuing series of violations' under a federal drug statute, supporting the argument that unanimity extends beyond the general verdict to specific factual findings.

A closely divided Court upheld a murder conviction where jurors may have disagreed on whether the defendant committed premeditated murder or felony murder, and both sides invoke it to support their competing visions of what the Constitution requires regarding juror agreement.

Established that any fact (other than a prior conviction) that increases the penalty beyond the prescribed statutory maximum must be submitted to a jury and proven beyond a reasonable doubt, reinforcing the argument that juror unanimity applies to factual findings that determine guilt.

Established that due process requires the prosecution to prove every element of a criminal offense beyond a reasonable doubt, which Kian argues is undermined when jurors may reach a unanimous verdict without individually agreeing on each element.

Extended Apprendi to require jury findings for sentencing enhancements under state guidelines, reinforcing the principle that factual determinations in criminal cases must be made by juries with proper constitutional safeguards.
